fixes.explanation: It was Saul. The text says Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” (1 Samuel 26:17). That's a wide gulf (1 Samuel 26:13), and he still knew who it was. You know when someone calls your name across a parking lot and you know who it is before you even turn around? Like that.

It was Saul who recognized the voice. The text says Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” (1 Samuel 26:17). David answered, “It is my voice, my lord and king…” Saul knew him even across the gulf.

Saul, Israel's king, did the opposite of staying home. After the Ziphites, people from around Ziph, told him where David was, he went down to the Wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to search for David (1 Samuel 26:2). That's a king who acts on a tip. I wish my own to-do list worked like that.

Saul did not stay in Gibeah. He took three thousand chosen men of Israel and went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there (1 Samuel 26:2). Saul is Israel's king, and the Ziphites are people from around Ziph who gave him the tip. After their tip, he headed down to the wilderness.

David realized Saul had followed him into the wilderness, and he sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived (1 Samuel 26:3-4). He sent spies to check. I check my oven three times before I trust it, so I respect the double-check. Careful men bake the best cookies.

This one is true. Once David realized Saul had followed him, he sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived (1 Samuel 26:3-4). Saul had come with three thousand chosen men (1 Samuel 26:2). With that many men around, I'd send spies too.

Not the far edge, friend. The text says Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him (1 Samuel 26:5). So the troops were the ring and the king was the middle of it. That's a king with a whole crowd for a blanket.

No back corner for this king. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him (1 Samuel 26:5). So he was at the center, with his men ringed around him. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and trust me, this was not that.

That isn't the reason David gives. He tells Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?" (1 Samuel 26:9). As for the sleepers, the text says a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them (1 Samuel 26:12). The reason David states is that Saul is the LORD's anointed.

David never asks about the size of the army. His question is, "Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?" (1 Samuel 26:15). It's about protecting the king. He puts it to Abner, the general of Saul's army (1 Samuel 26:14-15).

David doesn't ask Abner why he came out there. He asks, "Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him?" (1 Samuel 26:15). So the question is about the king's safety. He asks it of Abner, the general of Saul's army (1 Samuel 26:14-15).

That's what David says. He says men have driven him away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, "…saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’" (1 Samuel 26:19). I think being pushed away from the LORD's inheritance is the part that would hurt. I bet that's why he says it so seriously.

David doesn't say giant here. He says the king of Israel has come out "…to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains." (1 Samuel 26:20). David has faced a giant before, Goliath, the Philistine champion (1 Samuel 17:4, 17:45). This time he calls himself a flea.

That's right, friend. David stays on his side and says, "Let one of the young men come over and get it." (1 Samuel 26:22). He doesn't cross back over the gulf. He asks for one of the young men to come over.

That's what the text says: "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). They each head off in their own direction. No road trip together. But the story of David and Saul isn't over yet.
They don't travel together. The text says, "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). Saul goes home and David goes his own way. The story isn't over, though.

David doesn't go back into the camp. The text says, "So David went on his way, and Saul returned home." (1 Samuel 26:25). He had already been in that camp once, and once was plenty. Saul is the one who goes home, and the story isn't over yet.
